title: The Circular Economy
subtitle: Beyond the throwaway world
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: **Take, make, throw away**: that model is draining the planet. The circular economy proposes the opposite, keeping objects and materials in use for as long as possible.

hero.hook: What if waste simply did not exist? That is the bet of an economic model copied from nature.

blocks.text: Since the industrial revolution, our economy has run in one direction: we extract resources, we make objects, then we throw them away. The model assumes that resources are infinite. They are not.

The **circular economy** offers another logic, borrowed from nature, where nothing is truly lost. It aims to keep the value of products and materials in circulation as long as possible instead of turning them into waste.

sections.title: The linear model hits its limits

blocks.text: The modern economy was built on what is called a **linear** model: take, make, throw away. We pull raw materials out of nature, turn them into products, and once those products are worn out or out of fashion, they become waste.

blocks.caption: The “take, make, throw away” model assumes infinite resources

blocks.text: The system rests on the idea that resources are unlimited and that nature can absorb all the pollution. Yet the world economy now uses the resources of 1.7 planets every year. Some metals that digital technology cannot do without, such as [[Lithium]], could become hard to find as early as 2040.
Only 9% of all the plastic humanity has ever produced has been recycled. The rest ends up in nature or in landfill, where it can stay for 450 years.
The cost of cleaning up and managing waste is almost never included in the sale price of a product. It is a hidden cost, paid later by everyone.

The circular economy offers several loops, always in the same order of priority: the shortest loop is the best, because it wastes less energy and less material. Everything starts with **eco-design**, which means thinking about a product's environmental impact from the moment it is drawn, choosing durable materials that are easy to take apart.

Then comes **reuse** (an object changes owner without being transformed, as on a secondhand market), then **repair**, which extends a product's life. These steps fight directly against [[Planned obsolescence]], the practice of deliberately shortening the life of an object.

blocks.caption: Recycling comes last, after reuse and repair

blocks.text: **Recycling** comes only as a last resort. It still helps: recycling aluminum uses 95% less energy than extracting it from the raw ore, [[Bauxite]]. But it is always less efficient than simply reusing an object.

sections.title: Why it is still hard today

blocks.text: For all its promise, the circular economy runs into a simple problem: the linear model is often **cheaper in the short term**. Extracting new material sometimes costs less than sorting and recycling a complex piece of waste, especially when raw materials are cheap.

blocks.caption: The “right to repair” forces manufacturers to supply spare parts

blocks.text: Governments are stepping in more and more. In 2020 the European Union launched a plan that imposes stricter durability rules. One of its main pillars is the “right to repair,” which obliges makers of electronic devices to supply spare parts for several years.

Another lever is [[Extended Producer Responsibility]], which makes manufacturers pay for the waste their products create. That gives them a financial reason to design objects that pollute less and are easier to repair.

The circular economy is not only about recycling. It is a project for a society that consumes less and holds up better. By depending less on imported raw materials, a country also gains security in a more unstable world.

The success of this shift also depends on us, as consumers. The rule of the three Rs, reduce, reuse, recycle, starts with the first step: reduce, which means asking whether a purchase is really needed. That first move is the one with the biggest effect on the climate.
There is more gold in a ton of old smartphone circuit boards today than in a ton of ore dug out of a conventional gold mine.

The circular economy aims to break the “take, make, throw away” cycle by keeping resources in circulation through eco-design, repair and recycling, so that we live within the physical limits of our planet.
